let supplied = null;
try {
  const hook = $('AP Invoice Webhook').first().json;
  const body = hook && hook.body ? hook.body : hook;
  if (body && Array.isArray(body.invoices) && body.invoices.length) supplied = body.invoices;
} catch (e) {
  supplied = null;
}

if (supplied) {
  return supplied.map(function (r) {
    return { json: Object.assign({ source: 'webhook' }, r) };
  });
}

nodes.name: Collect Invoice Batch
nodes.notes: Uses the posted invoices from the webhook when there are any, otherwise emits the eleven demo invoices that exercise every branch, including two that try to bill a goods receipt twice.

nodes.name: Three-Way Match and Payment Engine
nodes.notes: Every rule that decides whether money leaves the company lives in this one node, in the order it is applied. The goods receipt is drawn down as it is billed, so quantity already invoiced against a PO — posted or earlier in this batch — can never be billed again.

nodes.name: Draft Journal Entry
nodes.notes: No human sees these. They post straight through and only appear in the run summary.

nodes.name: Write to Invoice Ledger
nodes.notes: Upsert on invoice_key. This row is what makes the same invoice a duplicate the next time it arrives, and qty_billed is what makes the goods receipt it drew on smaller for every run after this one.

parameters.content:
## 1 · Intake and master data

Invoices arrive on the webhook, or the demo batch stands in when the workflow is run by hand. The PO book, the goods receipts and the already-posted ledger are each read once per run and matched in memory — one query per invoice would be slower and would not make the answer any better.

Run **[PORTFOLIO] Reset AP Demo Ledger** before each demo run. The goods receipts are drawn down as invoices are accepted, so a second run on the same data legitimately finds the purchase orders already consumed and holds almost everything — correct behaviour, but not the picture you want to present cold.

## 2 · The decision

One node holds every rule, applied in a fixed order: field validation, duplicate guard, PO exists, goods actually received, quantity billed vs received, quantity vs PO, SKU, how much of that receipt is still open, then price against a 2% tolerance with a 50,000 IDR floor.

The goods receipt is drawn down, not re-read in full for every invoice. Quantity already invoiced — on the posted ledger and earlier in the same batch — is netted off first, so 600 units received cannot be billed 1,300 times over. Over-consumption is checked before price, because a receipt billed twice is a double payment, while a price is something procurement can still renegotiate.

What survives is routed by value: under 10M posts itself, under 100M needs a manager, above that a director. Payment terms are read at the same time, so 2/10 NET 30 produces a pay-by date that captures the discount.

## 3 · Three different pieces of paper

A clean small invoice becomes a journal entry nobody reads. A clean large one becomes a single approval message with the match evidence already in it. Anything that failed becomes a ticket addressed to the team that can actually fix it — warehouse, procurement, or AP.

## 4 · Record, then report

Every decision is written back to the ledger. Accepted invoices are keyed on vendor plus invoice number — that row is what catches the same invoice when the vendor sends it again next month.

Rejected ones are keyed on that plus the failure code, and the duplicate index is built only from accepted rows. Two reasons. A rejected duplicate must not overwrite the record of the payment it was checked against — the first version of this did exactly that, and after one run the ledger no longer knew the August invoice had been paid. And an invoice rejected for a price variance has to be payable once procurement fixes the PO, not rejected again as a duplicate.

If the write itself fails the run does not go quietly. A lost ledger row is the one fault that can lead to paying twice, so the write is not allowed to fail softly: a node-level failure stops the run outright rather than ending green with nothing recorded. A row can also go missing without the node erroring at all, so the summary counts only the rows the data table actually handed back, names any that are not there, and never reports a row as written when it was not.

nodes.name: Collect All Decisions
nodes.notes: Fan-in. Without this the ledger write, the summary, the report and the webhook response each ran once per branch instead of once per batch.

nodes.name: Ping the Approver in Slack
nodes.notes: Disabled on purpose. The approval text is already composed upstream; this is only where it lands. Pick a channel and a Slack credential to switch it on.

nodes.name: Email the Team That Owns It
nodes.notes: Disabled on purpose. Each exception already knows which team owns it, so the address is chosen from ticket_owner rather than sent to one shared inbox nobody reads.

nodes.name: Email the Morning AP Report
nodes.notes: Disabled on purpose. One message per run to the finance lead, not one per invoice.

parameters.content:
## 5 · Where it actually goes

All four are **switched off on purpose** and carry no credential, so the demo still runs for anyone who opens it with nothing to set up. They are wired as side branches, not in line — the invoice data reaches the ledger by exactly the same path whether they are on or off.

**Xero** takes the auto-approved bills as ACCPAY, status AUTHORISED, because only invoices that cleared the full three-way match under the touchless ceiling get this far. Line amounts carry **no tax** (`NoTax`), so the figure on the Xero bill is the same number the ledger records, the journal entry debits to `5-1200`, and the report shows. The other two settings both disagree with the journal entry: `Inclusive` splits that amount into net plus input tax and posts only the net to `5-1200`, and `Exclusive` adds PPN on top of it. If your AP is VAT-registered and you want the tax split, change the journal entry in the same branch to match.
**Slack** pings the one approver who has to look at it, with the match evidence already in the message.
**Gmail** sends each exception to the team that owns it — warehouse, procurement or AP — rather than to one shared inbox nobody reads, and sends the finance lead a single run report in the morning.

**Slack and Gmail** need a credential and a channel or address, and nothing else. **Xero needs three things and will not work with only a credential:** the tenant id of the organisation (the `organizationId` placeholder on the node), a Xero ContactID for the supplier — a GUID, not a name, so put a *Contact → Get Many* lookup in front of this node and have it set `xero_contact_id` — and an account code that exists in your chart of accounts. The node ships with `5-1200`, the same purchases account the journal entry in this branch debits; change both together if yours differs.

nodes.name: Post Bill to Xero
nodes.notes: Disabled on purpose, and it will not run on a credential alone. Three things must be supplied. organizationId is the Xero tenant id of the organisation and is required — the placeholder on the node is there to be replaced. contactId must be a Xero ContactID (a GUID); the vendor name will not resolve, so put a Contact > Get Many lookup in front of this node and have it set xero_contact_id, or paste the id over the placeholder. accountCode 5-1200 is the same purchases account the journal entry in this branch debits — change both together if your chart of accounts differs. Line amounts carry no tax (lineAmountType NoTax, taxType NONE), so the full invoice amount is what posts to 5-1200 — the same figure the ledger records, the journal entry debits and the report shows. The alternatives both disagree with the journal entry: Inclusive splits the amount into net plus input tax and posts only the net, and Exclusive adds PPN on top. If your AP is VAT-registered and you want the tax split, change the journal entry in this branch to match.
